commands.name: harness-issue

commands.name: harness-one

commands.name: harness-pause

commands.name: harness-plan

commands.name: harness-start

commands.name: harness-status

commands.name: harness-stop

commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

commands.name: debug
commands.description: Enable debug logging for this session and help diagnose issues

commands.name: code-review
commands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's recipe covers them) at the effort level given first, before any target (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings to many, some uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply them to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.

commands.name: simplify
commands.description: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

commands.name: batch
commands.description: Research and plan a large-scale change, then execute it in parallel across 5–30 isolated worktree agents that each open a PR.

commands.name: fewer-permission-prompts
commands.description: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.

commands.name: doctor
commands.description: Health-check the user's Claude Code setup and fix issues: diagnose installation health — what the `claude doctor` terminal diagnostics cover — from local data (duplicate or leftover installs, PATH, unparseable settings files, broken or colliding agent definitions, skills whose frontmatter fails to parse); find unused skills, MCP servers, and plugins versus their context cost and disable dead weight; deduplicate local CLAUDE.md files against checked-in ones; trim checked-in CLAUDE.md files by cutting content a session could derive from the codebase (directory layouts, tech-stack lists, architecture overviews) while keeping gotchas, rationale, and non-standard conventions; migrate always-loaded CLAUDE.md guidance into lazy skills and nested CLAUDE.md files; flag slow hooks and context-heavy extensions; check the installed version is current; make auto mode the default permission mode; and pre-approve frequently denied read-only commands. Use when the user asks for a doctor run, checkup, audit, tune-up, or cleanup of their Claude Code setup or configuration.

commands.name: loop
commands.description: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace.

commands.name: docs
commands.description: docs (editable docs people share and comment on; the default for any document, named as a doc or not: a document, report, proposal, resume, cover letter, letter, contract, policy, form, template, worksheet, essay, handbook, guide, how-to, cheat sheet, SOP or other writing to keep, share, collaborate on, send, submit, print or sign; a doc exports to Word, PDF, Markdown or Google Docs, so needing a file to send, attach, upload, submit or print is no reason to pick Word, and a file nobody asked for is a doc, not Word; a plan, comparison, summary or notes asked in chat stays in chat; a pasted claude.ai artifact link may be a doc: check with docs tools first; Word or another file format named, tracked changes wanted, or a .docx to change or use as a template → that format's skill): making one → if no docs-connector instructions are in context, call its `guide` (topic.instructions) first; then create the doc (headings only, no body) before any search, file read or plan, even with files attached. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: google-workspace
commands.description: Read this before the first Google Drive, Docs, Sheets or Slides connector call whenever the task creates or changes a Google file. Use this skill whenever the user wants to create or change a Google Doc, Sheet or Slides file in their Google Drive. Triggers include: a request that names Google Docs, Sheets, Slides or Drive and asks to make, edit, format, copy or rename a file; a docs.google.com link with a request to change that file, even a one-line fix or suggested edits; and any follow-up change to a Google file from earlier in the chat, even "change it" or "add a tab". Includes helper scripts for document positions, cell ranges and slide layout. However, if the user asks for a doc, deck or spreadsheet without naming Google, or gives a Google file only as source material for something new, use Claude's own output type instead. Do NOT use for read-only questions about a Google file, or for Word, Excel, PowerPoint or PDF files. (claude.ai sync)

(claude.ai sync)

commands.name: xlsx
commands.description: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: pptx
commands.description: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations as PowerPoint (.pptx) files; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email, summary, or creating a different type of slide deck); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user asks for a PowerPoint or .pptx file, or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. However, when the user asks for a deck, slides, a slide deck, or a presentation without naming a file format, default to using a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill if this session offers one; otherwise, use this skill. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: pdf
commands.description: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: docx
commands.description: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx) or Word templates (.dotx). Triggers include: any mention of Microsoft Word Documents, such as 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', 'microsoft doc'. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a deliverable as a Word or .docx file (to download, email or print), use this skill. However, if they ask for a document, page, report, memo, or notes WITHOUT naming a file format and the session offers Claude's own dedicated document or page skill or connector, use that instead, even if they will email or print it. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or coding unrelated to document generation. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: claude-api
commands.description:
Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read FIRST, before you answer, run a command or open a file (already started? read it now); don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

# Pennywise

I keep my household money in a plain text file and I'm tired of spreadsheets. I'd like a small
Python tool called **pennywise** that reads that file and tells me where the money went. It should
work two ways: as a library I can `import pennywise` from my own scripts, and as a `pennywise`
command I run in the terminal. Python 3.9 or newer, standard library only (no third-party
packages). Running `pip install .` in the project folder should give me both the importable
library and the `pennywise` command.

## The ledger file

One entry per line:

```
# household, March
2024-03-01 salary 2500.00 March pay
2024-03-02 groceries -42.50 weekly shop

2024-03-05 Rent -900
```

Each line has a date (`YYYY-MM-DD`), a category (one word), an amount, and an optional note. The
fields are separated by any amount of spaces or tabs. The note is the rest of the line exactly as I
wrote it (it can contain spaces), apart from trimming whitespace at both ends.

- A positive amount is money in, a negative one is money out. The sign is optional for money in, so
  `2500`, `+2500` and `2500.00` are all the same. Amounts have at most two decimal places: `12`,
  `12.5`, `-0.99` are fine; `12.505`, `1,000.00` and `abc` are not.
- Categories do not care about case: `Rent` and `rent` are the same category, and it is shown in
  lower case.
- Blank lines are ignored, and so are lines starting with `#`.
- Anything else is a mistake in my file, and the tool must tell me which line (counting from 1,
  blank and comment lines included). A date that does not exist, like `2024-02-30`, is a mistake
  too.

## Using it as a library

```python
import pennywise

entries = pennywise.parse(open("house.txt").read())
print(pennywise.balance(entries))
```

- `parse(text)` returns a list of entries, in the order they appear. Each entry has `.date` (a
  `datetime.date`), `.category` (a lower-case `str`), `.amount` (a `decimal.Decimal`) and `.note`
  (a `str`, empty when there is none).
- A bad line makes `parse` raise `pennywise.ParseError`. It is a `ValueError`, its `.line`
  attribute is the line number, and its message mentions `line N`.
- `balance(entries)` is the total of all amounts, a `Decimal` (zero for no entries).
- `by_category(entries)` is a `dict` of category to its total; `by_month(entries)` is the same
  keyed by month, like `"2024-03"`.
- `filter_entries(entries, category=None, since=None, until=None)` returns the matching entries in
  the order given. `category` is matched without regard to case; `since` and `until` are
  `datetime.date` values and both ends are included. Anything left as `None` is not filtered on.

## Using it from the terminal

```
$ pennywise balance house.txt
1457.50

$ pennywise summary house.txt
groceries  -42.50
rent  -900.00
salary  2500.00

$ pennywise list house.txt --category groceries
2024-03-02 groceries -42.50 weekly shop
```

- `pennywise balance FILE` prints the total with two decimals, on one line.
- `pennywise summary FILE [--by category|month]` prints one line per group, sorted by name: the
  name, some spaces, then the total with two decimals. The default is `--by category`.
- `pennywise list FILE [--category C] [--since DATE] [--until DATE]` prints the matching entries,
  oldest first (entries on the same day keep the order of the file), one per line as
  `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT NOTE`. The amount always has two decimals, and the note (and the space
  before it) is left out when there is none.
- `pennywise add FILE DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]` adds an entry to the end of the file (creating
  the file if it does not exist) and prints the line it added, written the same way `list` writes
  it. I pass the note as a single quoted argument. An invalid entry is refused and the file is left
  exactly as it was.
- `pennywise export FILE [--format csv]` prints the entries, in the same order as `list`, as CSV
  with the header `date,category,amount,note`. CSV is the only format for now and the default.
- `balance`, `summary` and `list` take `--json` to print JSON instead. Amounts are strings with two
  decimals: `{"balance": "1457.50"}`, `{"groceries": "-42.50", "rent": "-900.00"}`, and for `list`
  an array of `{"date": "2024-03-02", "category": "groceries", "amount": "-42.50", "note":
  "weekly shop"}`.
- Wherever a command reads a file (not `add`), `-` means read the ledger from standard input.
- Exit status: `0` when it worked; `1` when the ledger (or the entry given to `add`) has a mistake,
  with a message on standard error that names the line and nothing on standard output; `2` when
  the file cannot be read or the command line is wrong (no command, an unknown command, a bad
  option value, a date I mistyped).

## Problem Statement

The user keeps household money in a plain-text ledger file and is tired of spreadsheets. They want a small, dependency-free Python tool, **pennywise**, that parses the ledger and reports where the money went — usable both as an importable library (`import pennywise`) and as a `pennywise` terminal command.

## Solution

A pure-stdlib Python package (Python >= 3.9) installable with `pip install .`, providing:

- a library API: `parse`, `ParseError`, `Entry`, `balance`, `by_category`, `by_month`, `filter_entries`;
- a `pennywise` console script (and `python -m pennywise`) with subcommands `balance`, `summary`, `list`, `add`, `export`, `--json` output for `balance`/`summary`/`list`, `-` for stdin, and well-defined exit codes (0 ok / 1 ledger or entry mistake / 2 unreadable file or bad command line).

## User Stories

1. As a user, I `import pennywise` and call `pennywise.parse(text)` to get a list of entries with `.date`, `.category`, `.amount`, `.note`.
2. As a user, when my file has a mistake, I get a `pennywise.ParseError` (a `ValueError`) whose `.line` and message tell me which line (counting blank/comment lines).
3. As a user, I get the balance, per-category totals and per-month totals as `Decimal`s.
4. As a user, I filter entries by category (case-insensitive) and an inclusive date range.
5. As a user, I run `pennywise balance|summary|list FILE` in the terminal, optionally with `--json`, and read from stdin with `-`.
6. As a user, I run `pennywise add FILE DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]` to append a validated entry; invalid entries leave the file byte-for-byte unchanged.
7. As a user, I run `pennywise export FILE` to get CSV.
8. As a scripter, I rely on exit codes 0/1/2 and on stdout being empty on error.

## Implementation Decisions

Layout (src layout, setuptools, no third-party runtime deps):

- `pyproject.toml` — `[build-system] requires = ["setuptools>=61"]`, `build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"`; `[project] name = "pennywise"`, `requires-python = ">=3.9"`, `dependencies = []`; `[project.scripts] pennywise = "pennywise.cli:main"`; package discovery under `src/`.
- `src/pennywise/__init__.py` — re-exports `Entry, ParseError, parse, balance, by_category, by_month, filter_entries` (`__all__`).
- `src/pennywise/ledger.py` — parsing + aggregation (library core).
- `src/pennywise/cli.py` — argparse CLI, `main(argv=None) -> int` (console script calls `sys.exit(main())`).
- `src/pennywise/__main__.py` — `python -m pennywise`.
- `tests/` — stdlib `unittest` only (`python -m unittest discover -s tests`). No pytest dependency required (tests must also pass under pytest if present).

Parsing rules (decided):

- Lines are split with `str.splitlines()`; line numbers count from 1 including blank and comment lines.
- A line is **blank** if `line.strip() == ""`. A line is a **comment** if `line.lstrip()` starts with `#` (leading whitespace before `#` is allowed).
- Otherwise the line is split as `line.strip().split(None, 3)` (spaces/tabs, any amount). Fewer than 3 fields → error. Field 4 (if present) is the note, already stripped at both ends; the note's internal whitespace is preserved exactly.
- Date: must match `^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$` AND be a real calendar date (`datetime.date(y, m, d)`); `2024-02-30` and `2024-3-5` are errors.
- Category: any single non-whitespace token, stored `.lower()`.
- Amount: must fully match `^[+-]?\d+(\.\d{1,2})?$` (so `12`, `+12`, `12.5`, `-0.99`, `2500.00` ok; `12.505`, `1,000.00`, `abc`, `.5`, `5.`, `1e3` rejected). Stored as `Decimal(text)` (not re-quantized).
- `ParseError(ValueError)` constructed as `ParseError(line, reason)`; `.line` is the int line number; `str(err)` is `"line N: <reason>"`.
- `Entry` is a frozen `dataclass(date: datetime.date, category: str, amount: Decimal, note: str = "")`.

- `balance(entries)` → `sum(amounts, Decimal(0))`; `Decimal("0")` for no entries. Accepts any iterable.
- `by_category(entries)` / `by_month(entries)` → plain `dict[str, Decimal]`, keys inserted in sorted order. Month key is `f"{d.year:04d}-{d.month:02d}"`.
- `filter_entries(entries, category=None, since=None, until=None)` → new list, input order preserved; category compared with `.lower()` on both sides; `since <= date <= until`.

CLI (decided):

- Formatting money: `format(amount, ".2f")` via `Decimal.quantize(Decimal("0.01"))`; **never print `-0.00`** (normalize zero to `0.00`).
- `balance FILE [--json]` → `1457.50` / `{"balance": "1457.50"}`.
- `summary FILE [--by {category,month}] [--json]` → one line per group sorted by name, format `f"{name}  {total}"` (two spaces). Empty ledger prints nothing (JSON: `{}`). `--by` with any other value → argparse error, exit 2.
- `list FILE [--category C] [--since DATE] [--until DATE] [--json]` → stable sort by date (same-day entries keep file order), lines `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT[ NOTE]`. JSON: array of `{"date","category","amount","note"}` (note `""` when absent), `[]` when empty. `--since/--until` parsed with the same strict date rule; a malformed or nonexistent date → exit 2 with an argparse-style usage error.
- `add FILE DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]`:
  - Builds the candidate line and validates it with the same parser rules (date, category must be one non-empty token without whitespace, amount regex; note must not contain a newline). Invalid → exit **1**, message on stderr, nothing on stdout, file untouched (not even created).   - The written line is the canonical `list` format (lower-case category, 2-decimal amount, note omitted when empty or whitespace-only; note stripped).
  - Appends with UTF-8; if the file exists, is non-empty and does not end with a newline, a `\n` is written first. Creates the file if missing. Prints the written line. The existing content is not re-validated.
  - Negative amounts like `-42.50` must work as a positional argument (argparse treats them as positionals when no option looks like a negative number — keep it that way; add a test).
  - `add` does not accept `-` as stdin.
  - Parent directory missing / unwritable → exit 2.
- `export FILE [--format csv]` → `csv.writer` with `lineterminator="\n"`, header `date,category,amount,note`, rows in `list` order, amount 2 decimals. `--format` choices `["csv"]` only (other → exit 2).
- `-` as FILE reads `sys.stdin` (for balance/summary/list/export).
- Files read as UTF-8. Missing file, a directory, permission denied, or undecodable bytes → exit 2, message `pennywise: cannot read FILE: ...` on stderr.
- ParseError → exit 1, stderr `pennywise: FILE: line N: reason` (FILE shown as `<stdin>` for `-`), stdout empty. Compute all output before printing anything, so stdout stays empty on error.
- No command / unknown command / bad option → argparse exits 2 (usage on stderr). `main()` must return int codes rather than raising for handled errors; `SystemExit` from argparse is allowed to propagate its code.

## Testing Decisions

- stdlib `unittest` in `tests/test_ledger.py` (library) and `tests/test_cli.py` (CLI via `main(argv)` with captured stdout/stderr, plus at least one subprocess test via `python -m pennywise`).

- Any output formats other than CSV for export; any third-party packages; currencies; editing/deleting entries; config files; Python < 3.9.

- [ ] `pip install .` (stdlib only, Python >= 3.9) installs the importable `pennywise` package and the `pennywise` console command; `python -m pennywise` also works.
- [ ] `parse(text)` returns entries in file order with `.date` (`datetime.date`), `.category` (lower-case `str`), `.amount` (`Decimal`), `.note` (`str`, `""` when absent; rest of line, trimmed at both ends, internal spacing preserved); fields split on any run of spaces/tabs.

A pure-stdlib Python package (Python >= 3.9) installable with `pip install .`, providing:

- a library API: `parse`, `ParseError`, `Entry`, `balance`, `by_category`, `by_month`, `filter_entries`;
- a `pennywise` console script (and `python -m pennywise`) with subcommands `balance`, `summary`, `list`, `add`, `export`, `--json` output for `balance`/`summary`/`list`, `-` for stdin, and well-defined exit codes (0 ok / 1 ledger or entry mistake / 2 unreadable file or bad command line).

## User Stories

1. As a user, I `import pennywise` and call `pennywise.parse(text)` to get a list of entries with `.date`, `.category`, `.amount`, `.note`.
2. As a user, when my file has a mistake, I get a `pennywise.ParseError` (a `ValueError`) whose `.line` and message tell me which line (counting blank/comment lines).
3. As a user, I get the balance, per-category totals and per-month totals as `Decimal`s.
4. As a user, I filter entries by category (case-insensitive) and an inclusive date range.
5. As a user, I run `pennywise balance|summary|list FILE` in the terminal, optionally with `--json`, and read from stdin with `-`.
6. As a user, I run `pennywise add FILE DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]` to append a validated entry; invalid entries leave the file byte-for-byte unchanged.
7. As a user, I run `pennywise export FILE` to get CSV.
8. As a scripter, I rely on exit codes 0/1/2 and on stdout being empty on error.

## Implementation Decisions

Layout (src layout, setuptools, no third-party runtime deps):

- `pyproject.toml` — `[build-system] requires = ["setuptools>=61"]`, `build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"`; `[project] name = "pennywise"`, `requires-python = ">=3.9"`, `dependencies = []`; `[project.scripts] pennywise = "pennywise.cli:main"`; package discovery under `src/`.
- `src/pennywise/__init__.py` — re-exports `Entry, ParseError, parse, balance, by_category, by_month, filter_entries` (`__all__`).
- `src/pennywise/ledger.py` — parsing + aggregation (library core).
- `src/pennywise/cli.py` — argparse CLI, `main(argv=None) -> int` (console script calls `sys.exit(main())`).
- `src/pennywise/__main__.py` — `python -m pennywise`.
- `tests/` — stdlib `unittest` only (`python -m unittest discover -s tests`). No pytest dependency required (tests must also pass under pytest if present).

Parsing rules (decided):

- Lines are split with `str.splitlines()`; line numbers count from 1 including blank and comment lines.
- A line is **blank** if `line.strip() == ""`. A line is a **comment** if `line.lstrip()` starts with `#` (leading whitespace before `#` is allowed).
- Otherwise the line is split as `line.strip().split(None, 3)` (spaces/tabs, any amount). Fewer than 3 fields → error. Field 4 (if present) is the note, already stripped at both ends; the note's internal whitespace is preserved exactly.
- Date: must match `^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$` AND be a real calendar date (`datetime.date(y, m, d)`); `2024-02-30` and `2024-3-5` are errors.
- Category: any single non-whitespace token, stored `.lower()`.
- Amount: must fully match `^[+-]?\d+(\.\d{1,2})?$` (so `12`, `+12`, `12.5`, `-0.99`, `2500.00` ok; `12.505`, `1,000.00`, `abc`, `.5`, `5.`, `1e3` rejected). Stored as `Decimal(text)` (not re-quantized).
- `ParseError(ValueError)` constructed as `ParseError(line, reason)`; `.line` is the int line number; `str(err)` is `"line N: <reason>"`.
- `Entry` is a frozen `dataclass(date: datetime.date, category: str, amount: Decimal, note: str = "")`.

Aggregation:

- `balance(entries)` → `sum(amounts, Decimal(0))`; `Decimal("0")` for no entries. Accepts any iterable.
- `by_category(entries)` / `by_month(entries)` → plain `dict[str, Decimal]`, keys inserted in sorted order. Month key is `f"{d.year:04d}-{d.month:02d}"`.
- `filter_entries(entries, category=None, since=None, until=None)` → new list, input order preserved; category compared with `.lower()` on both sides; `since <= date <= until`.

CLI (decided):

- Formatting money: `format(amount, ".2f")` via `Decimal.quantize(Decimal("0.01"))`; **never print `-0.00`** (normalize zero to `0.00`).
- `balance FILE [--json]` → `1457.50` / `{"balance": "1457.50"}`.
- `summary FILE [--by {category,month}] [--json]` → one line per group sorted by name, format `f"{name}  {total}"` (two spaces). Empty ledger prints nothing (JSON: `{}`). `--by` with any other value → argparse error, exit 2.
- `list FILE [--category C] [--since DATE] [--until DATE] [--json]` → stable sort by date (same-day entries keep file order), lines `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT[ NOTE]`. JSON: array of `{"date","category","amount","note"}` (note `""` when absent), `[]` when empty. `--since/--until` parsed with the same strict date rule; a malformed or nonexistent date → exit 2 with an argparse-style usage error.
- `add FILE DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]`:
  - Builds the candidate line and validates it with the same parser rules (date, category must be one non-empty token without whitespace, amount regex; note must not contain a newline). Invalid → exit **1**, message on stderr, nothing on stdout, file untouched (not even created). (Decision: a bad DATE given to `add` is an entry mistake → exit 1; "a date I mistyped" → exit 2 applies to `--since/--until`.)
  - The written line is the canonical `list` format (lower-case category, 2-decimal amount, note omitted when empty or whitespace-only; note stripped).
  - Appends with UTF-8; if the file exists, is non-empty and does not end with a newline, a `\n` is written first. Creates the file if missing. Prints the written line. The existing content is not re-validated.
  - Negative amounts like `-42.50` must work as a positional argument (argparse treats them as positionals when no option looks like a negative number — keep it that way; add a test).
  - `add` does not accept `-` as stdin.
  - Parent directory missing / unwritable → exit 2.
- `export FILE [--format csv]` → `csv.writer` with `lineterminator="\n"`, header `date,category,amount,note`, rows in `list` order, amount 2 decimals. `--format` choices `["csv"]` only (other → exit 2).
- `-` as FILE reads `sys.stdin` (for balance/summary/list/export).
- Files read as UTF-8. Missing file, a directory, permission denied, or undecodable bytes → exit 2, message `pennywise: cannot read FILE: ...` on stderr.
- ParseError → exit 1, stderr `pennywise: FILE: line N: reason` (FILE shown as `<stdin>` for `-`), stdout empty. Compute all output before printing anything, so stdout stays empty on error.
- No command / unknown command / bad option → argparse exits 2 (usage on stderr). `main()` must return int codes rather than raising for handled errors; `SystemExit` from argparse is allowed to propagate its code.

## Testing Decisions

- stdlib `unittest` in `tests/test_ledger.py` (library) and `tests/test_cli.py` (CLI via `main(argv)` with captured stdout/stderr, plus at least one subprocess test via `python -m pennywise`).
- Cover every acceptance criterion below, including edge cases: tabs as separators, note with internal multiple spaces, leading/trailing whitespace, `2024-02-30`, `12.505`, `1,000.00`, `+2500`, same-day ordering in `list`, `-0.00` avoidance, stdin `-`, `add` refusing leaves file byte-identical and not created, `add` to file with no trailing newline, exit codes 0/1/2 and empty stdout on error.
- Verify `pip install .` in a fresh venv yields both `import pennywise` and the `pennywise` command.

## Out of Scope

- Any output formats other than CSV for export; any third-party packages; currencies; editing/deleting entries; config files; Python < 3.9.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `pip install .` (stdlib only, Python >= 3.9) installs the importable `pennywise` package and the `pennywise` console command; `python -m pennywise` also works.
- [ ] `parse(text)` returns entries in file order with `.date` (`datetime.date`), `.category` (lower-case `str`), `.amount` (`Decimal`), `.note` (`str`, `""` when absent; rest of line, trimmed at both ends, internal spacing preserved); fields split on any run of spaces/tabs.
- [ ] Amount accepts an optional sign and at most two decimals (`2500`, `+2500`, `2500.00`, `12.5`, `-0.99`); rejects `12.505`, `1,000.00`, `abc`.
- [ ] Blank lines and lines starting with `#` are ignored; any other malformed line (including nonexistent dates like `2024-02-30`) raises `pennywise.ParseError`, a `ValueError`, with `.line` = 1-based line number (blank/comment lines counted) and a message containing `line N`.
- [ ] `balance` returns a `Decimal` total (zero for no entries); `by_category` and `by_month` (`"YYYY-MM"`) return `dict`s of `Decimal` totals.
- [ ] `filter_entries(entries, category=None, since=None, until=None)` preserves order, matches category case-insensitively, includes both date ends, and ignores `None` filters.
- [ ] `pennywise balance FILE` prints the total with two decimals on one line.
- [ ] `pennywise summary FILE [--by category|month]` prints one sorted line per group: name, spaces, total with two decimals; default `--by category`.
- [ ] `pennywise list FILE [--category C] [--since DATE] [--until DATE]` prints matching entries oldest first (same-day keeps file order) as `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT[ NOTE]`, amount with two decimals, note and its space omitted when empty.
- [ ] `pennywise add FILE DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]` appends the entry (creating the file if needed), prints the added line in `list` format; an invalid entry is refused with exit 1 and the file is left exactly as it was.
- [ ] `pennywise export FILE [--format csv]` prints CSV with header `date,category,amount,note`, rows in `list` order.
- [ ] `--json` on `balance`/`summary`/`list` prints JSON with amounts as 2-decimal strings, in the shapes given in the original request.
- [ ] `-` as FILE reads the ledger from stdin for every reading command.
- [ ] Exit status: 0 on success; 1 on a ledger/`add` entry mistake with a stderr message naming the line and empty stdout; 2 when the file cannot be read or the command line is wrong (no command, unknown command, bad option value, mistyped `--since/--until` date).
- [ ] Unit + CLI tests (stdlib `unittest`) cover all of the above and pass.
